title: The life cycle, reviewed
hook: from the adhan in the ear to the last prayer

segments.voice: Yesterday, the manners, and your line: courtesy. A boy at a platter, three small instructions, kept for life. Which small adab did you keep on purpose? Day one thousand four hundred eighteen.

A grandfather leans over a newborn, hours old, and whispers the call to prayer into the baby's right ear. Allahu akbar. The baby is not going to stand up and pray. There is no prayer after this call. Long afterward, rows of people stand in a mosque courtyard for a funeral prayer. There is no call before that prayer. Some Muslims put the two together in a saying people repeat: a life is the space between a call and its prayer. Today, the life cycle again, from the adhan in the ear to the last prayer.
screen: `A CALL WHISPERED IN A NEWBORN'S EAR.` → `A PRAYER WITH NO CALL BEFORE IT.` → `A LIFE IN BETWEEN.`

segments.voice: First, the beginning. A report in Abu Dawud's collection, in paraphrase, says the Prophet, peace be upon him, gave the call to prayer in the ear of his grandson Hasan when he was born. In Sahih al-Bukhari, a companion brings his newborn son to the Prophet, who names him, chews a date, and touches it to the baby's mouth. A good name, a taste of sweetness, and in some families a sacrifice shared in thanks. Second, childhood. A report in Abu Dawud tells parents to have their children pray from the age of seven: learning by doing, beside the people who love them. Third, marriage and home. The year called the nikah a contract of mercy: consent, witnesses, and a gift to the bride that belongs to her alone, which the Qur'an tells husbands to give, in paraphrase. Fourth, illness and death. In Sahih al-Bukhari, in paraphrase, the Prophet tells his followers to feed the hungry, visit the sick and free the captive. A sick room is a place to go toward, not to avoid. And at a loss, the Qur'an gives the words people say: "Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning." Then the funeral prayer, said standing, in rows, for someone who can no longer stand. Customs differ between cultures and schools at every step. But the shape stays: every stage has its words, and every stage has people around it.
screen: `A CALL, A NAME, A TASTE OF DATE.` · `CHILDREN LEARN BY PRAYING BESIDE YOU.` · `A CONTRACT OF MERCY.` · `VISIT THE SICK; SAY THE WORDS OF RETURN.`

segments.voice: The practice: pray for someone at each stage. Settle into the sit, and breathe. Walk the stages slowly, one person at each. A new baby you know of. A child learning. A couple, newly married or long married. Someone who is sick right now. Someone who has died. Give each one a few breaths of your attention. If you pray, you can ask good for each of them in your own words. If you don't, simply hold each face in mind, one after another. The bell holds the time.
The life cycle. From the call in a newborn's ear to the funeral prayer, each stage with its own words and its own people. Today's word.

Your line: every stage. Today, reach one person at a stage that is hard right now: a new parent, someone sick, someone grieving. A message is enough. Tomorrow, the world, reviewed. Day one thousand four hundred eighteen.

howItsDone: Muslim families mark each stage with practices drawn from hadith and local custom: the call to prayer in a newborn's ear, naming and the 'aqiqah, teaching children to pray, the nikah contract, visiting the sick, and washing, shrouding and praying the funeral prayer for the dead.
